_readme: Model v3 — the fit-profile matcher, written from the job-search matching specification. This is an OVERLAY on config/profile.json, like profile.v2.json: search terms, engagement, skills, penalties, location and the exclusion list are inherited, and only what defines this model lives here. v3 does not score one blended number out of a title and some keywords. It scores four separate axes — WORK FIT (what she would actually do all day), EXPERIENCE FIT (how much of that work she has already done), QUALIFICATION FIT (the employer's stated requirements) and LIFESTYLE FIT (remote, contract, flexibility) — and weights them 35/30/20/15 into the overall score. The bands, the recommendation, the learnable-vs-true gap split and the freshness rules are all from the spec.

search._comment: Quality over quantity: this board publishes far fewer postings than v1 and v2. minMatchScore sits just under the spec's 70-point 'possible adjacent opportunity' band so near-misses stay reachable with the slider, and everything below that is dropped rather than stored.
search._freshnessComment: The spec hides anything over 30 days by default unless it is unusually strong. staleAfterDays is that cutoff; a posting older than it survives only by scoring staleKeepMinMatch or better, and is labelled as needing its availability confirmed.

ranking._comment: Freshness is 'extremely important' per the spec, so the half-life is shorter here than on the other boards and the bucket bonuses below sharpen it further. These adjust the sort order only — never the score, which has to keep meaning what the bands say it means.

_axisWeightsComment: The spec's weighting, and the only place it is defined.
_workGateComment: WORK FIT IS THE GATE. The other three axes have high floors by their nature — every posting on this board is remote (lifestyle), she clears most stated requirements (qualification), and she has done a great deal of adjacent work (experience). Weighted together those three are 65% of the score, so without this a job she has no wish to do reached the apply bands on being qualified for it: a marine sales role scored 72 on work fit 39, and a UX/UI design contract led the board at 85. The cap says the obvious thing — a job she does not want to do cannot be a strong match however well she would meet its requirements — and lets the axis the specification calls primary actually decide. base + slope*100 must reach 100 so a perfect posting is never capped.
_bandsComment: The spec's result labels, highest first. `recommendation` is what the card prints as the call to action.
_freshnessBucketsComment: Sort-order bonuses only. maxDays is inclusive; the last bucket catches everything older.

freshnessBuckets.label: Posted in the last two weeks
Over a month old — confirm it is still open

_roleFamiliesComment: The spec's highest-priority job families. `tier` decides how much a title alone is worth: `core` families are the ones to search aggressively for, `priority` are close variations, `adjacent` are the ones she would not think to search — those are flagged as new directions on the card and carry `why` to explain themselves. Titles here are matched against the job title only; the description does the rest of the work.

roleFamilies.label: Content & editorial quality
roleFamilies.why: Reviewing content somebody else produced, against a standard, before it goes out — the exact shape of your last ten years.

roleFamilies.label: Marketing & digital editing
roleFamilies.why: Editing marketing and web content written by others — your ten years of reviewing customer-facing campaign copy reads as direct experience, not a transfer.

roleFamilies.label: Copy editing & proofreading
roleFamilies.why: The craft itself: someone else writes it, you make it correct.

roleFamilies.label: Email, CRM & campaign QA
roleFamilies.why: Your incumbent job, named the way employers name it.

roleFamilies.label: E-commerce & product content
roleFamilies.why: Checking product names, pricing, offers and terminology against a source of truth is what you already do for retail campaigns — the same work, one system further upstream.

roleFamilies.label: Production & final review
roleFamilies.why: The last pair of eyes before publication, and the workflow that gets it there — your production QA habit with an editorial title on it.

roleFamilies.label: Educational & assessment content
roleFamilies.why: An honours degree in English and two years as a university Instructor of Record — building, teaching and assessing a curriculum — on top of the same review discipline. Educational publishers and assessment teams are hiring exactly this.

roleFamilies.label: Review & compliance work under another name
roleFamilies.why: Checking documents against a written rule, at volume, without missing anything — the same discipline as brand-guideline QA, in teams that never advertise for an editor.

_workSignalTiersComment: CORE signals are evidence that the job is reviewing work somebody else produced, against a standard: proofreading, review and sign-off, accuracy and verification, working to a style guide, content audit. SUPPORTING signals say where and with whom — channels, product content, layout, detail, collaboration, workflow, learning content — and are context, not evidence. Every digital and creative posting carries the supporting vocabulary, so before this split a Creative Designer scored 80 on work fit and a payroll role 79. Supporting signals are now capped at supportingCap of the 46 available, and a posting with no core signal at all cannot exceed noCoreCap, because nothing in it says she would be reviewing anything.
_workSignalsComment: THE PRIMARY AXIS. The spec is explicit that titles must not be trusted on their own — 'what would this person actually spend her day doing?' Each group is a concept from the spec's high-value description signals, matched anywhere in the posting, with diminishing returns so a posting that stuffs one concept cannot beat one that genuinely describes the work.

workSignals.label: Accuracy, verification and discrepancy detection
workSignals._comment: A bare 'accuracy'/'accurate'/'errors' matched every posting on the board — payroll, sales and engineering alike. The phrases here name reviewing something for accuracy rather than merely being accurate at your own job.

workSignals.label: Working to a style guide and brand standards
Content audit and validation
workSignals._comment: A bare 'audit'/'auditing' was removed: it is finance and compliance vocabulary, and it gave a payroll specialist the same core signal as a content audit. Every phrase here now names the thing being audited.

workSignals.label: Customer-facing email, web and campaign content
Feedback to designers, developers and production teams

_combinationsComment: The spec's VERY STRONG COMBINATIONS, and its instruction that these matter more than an exact title match. Each entry needs one phrase from every list, anywhere in the posting, in any order. EVERY MEMBER MUST NAME ITS OWN CONCEPT: a set containing a bare 'review', 'quality', 'audit' or 'compare' turns "concepts appearing together" into "common words appearing together", which is how a Sr. Global Payroll Specialist came to fire both 'Email + content review + quality assurance' and 'Content audit + discrepancies + source of truth'. Total is capped so a long posting cannot collect all fourteen.

combinations.label: Content audit + discrepancies + source of truth

_orientationComment: The spec's central question about writing: IS THE PERSON PRIMARILY CREATING THE CONTENT, OR REVIEWING CONTENT CREATED BY OTHERS? A posting is not rejected for mentioning writing — editing roles rewrite sentences all the time. It is scored on the balance. Distinct concepts are counted on each side; whichever dominates moves the work-fit score, and a creation-dominant posting also earns a 'watch out for' note.

orientation._creationTitlesComment: A title is the strongest available statement of what the primary responsibility is, which is exactly the question the spec asks about writing. A posting called 'Copywriter' is a writing job however much reviewing its description also mentions, so the title carries its own penalty on top of the balance below.

_automationComment: The spec's other negative: she does not want to become an automation engineer or a developer. Technical literacy is a positive and is never penalised here — HTML, CSS and reading templates are her daily tools, and they live in workSignals and skills. Only writing code as the job is penalised.
_experienceComment: EXPERIENCE FIT — the spec's transferable-experience logic, made mechanical. Each entry is work she has demonstrably performed; `phrases` are how a posting asks for it, and `evidence` is the sentence the card offers as YOUR STRONGEST EVIDENCE, ready to lift into an application. Experience fit is a coverage ratio: of everything this posting asks for, how much has she already done? That is what stops a job being rejected because the title differs, and what stops a job being credited for work she has never done.

experience.label: HTML email and campaign QA
experience.evidence: Ten years of QA on HTML email and web campaigns for major retail and e-commerce brands, checking rendering, links, offers and copy before deployment.

experience.label: Professional proofreading and copy editing
experience.evidence: Proofread customer-facing copy daily for ten years — spelling, grammar, punctuation, capitalization, hyphenation, trademarks and product terminology — as the last review before publication.

experience.label: Applying style guides and brand conventions
experience.evidence: Applied client-specific style guides and brand conventions across several concurrent retail brands, keeping each one internally consistent and consistent with its own live site.

experience.label: Checking content against a source of truth
experience.evidence: Investigated inconsistencies by comparing campaign assets against the live site, previous campaigns and product data — determining the correct treatment from evidence, and escalating rather than guessing when the evidence did not settle it.

experience.label: Visual and layout quality assurance
experience.evidence: Caught spacing, alignment, imagery, alt-text and broken-link faults across email and web builds — visual QA alongside the editorial pass, not instead of it.

experience.label: Retail product and pricing content
experience.evidence: Verified product names, terminology, pricing and offers against source data for retail e-commerce campaigns — the same checks a product-content or catalog QA role runs, one system upstream.

experience.label: Concise defect feedback to designers and developers
experience.evidence: Delivered concise, actionable QA feedback to designers and developers in a fast-paced agency production cycle, which is what kept rework down.
experience._comment: 'collaborate', 'stakeholders', 'cross-functional' and a bare 'feedback' are in every posting on the board and were credited as her experience on all of them.

experience.label: Many concurrent projects to deadline
experience.evidence: Ran QA on many concurrent campaigns against a production schedule, prioritising by launch date without letting a deadline slip.
experience._comment: 'deadlines', 'fast-paced', 'prioritize' and 'organizational skills' were removed: every posting ever written contains them, and an entry that matches everything measures nothing.

experience.label: Teaching, curriculum and assessment
experience.evidence: Instructor of Record at university level: built a semester's curriculum to stated objectives, taught it, and developed and evaluated the material and the assessments that went with it.

experience.label: Formal training in English language and literature
experience.evidence: Honours degree in English Language and Literature, plus a graduate degree and university teaching in language and literature — the formal grounding these postings ask for when they say 'degree in English, Journalism or Communications'.

experience.label: Reviewing content in HTML and CMS environments
experience.evidence: Comfortable reading and reviewing HTML directly and working inside CMS and campaign tools — technical literacy without wanting a developer's job.

experience._comment: Deliberately narrow. This entry used to match 'remote', 'contract' and 'collaborate', which is every posting on a remote job board — it credited a marine sales role with her experience and pushed the whole board's experience fit into the nineties. Remote and contract are scored on the lifestyle axis, where they belong; what is left here is the part that is actually evidence.
experience.label: Remote, self-directed delivery
experience.evidence: Ten years of remote work, including freelance and project-based engagements delivered against a brief with minimal supervision.

_experienceGapsComment: Demands she has NOT performed. These are the other half of the experience-fit ratio — a posting that asks for five things she has done and none of these scores near the top, and one that asks mostly for these does not, however friendly its title. Kept separate from qualification gaps because these are about the work itself, not about a stated requirement.

experienceGaps.label: Legal editing or a legal qualification
Newsroom reporting
experienceGaps._comment: Bare 'reporting' is deliberately absent — every marketing posting on the board mentions reporting, and it was filing ordinary coordinator roles as newsroom work.

experienceGaps.label: Software engineering
experienceGaps._comment: 'code review' and 'version control' are absent on purpose: documentation and CMS roles use both, and neither means the job is engineering.

experienceGaps.label: Paid media buying and analytics ownership

_qualificationComment: QUALIFICATION FIT — how closely she meets what the employer explicitly asks for. The base is high on purpose: ten years in the work, an honours BA and a graduate degree clear the stated bar for most of these postings. What moves it is the specific asks. The spec's rule holds here — one easily learnable missing tool must not destroy the score, so learnable gaps cost a few points each and are reported separately from the ones that genuinely disqualify.

learnableGaps.label: AP Style
learnableGaps.note: A style manual, not a discipline — you have a decade of applying client style guides and can absorb AP in a weekend.

learnableGaps.label: Chicago Manual of Style
learnableGaps.note: Same again: a specific manual on top of ten years of enforcing house style.

learnableGaps.label: A specific style manual (MLA / APA / AMA)
learnableGaps.note: Manual-specific conventions layered on existing style-guide discipline.

learnableGaps.label: A specific CMS
learnableGaps.note: You have worked in CMS and campaign tools; the platform name changes, the work does not.

learnableGaps.label: A PIM platform such as Salsify
learnableGaps.note: Product-information tooling around work you already do by hand against source data.

learnableGaps.label: A specific e-commerce platform
learnableGaps.note: Retail e-commerce content is familiar ground; the storefront platform is a tool to learn.

learnableGaps.label: A specific editorial tool
learnableGaps.note: Terminology and linting tools sit on top of the editorial judgement they automate.

learnableGaps.label: Assessment-development terminology
learnableGaps.note: Item banks, DOK levels and alignment vocabulary — new words for curriculum and evaluation work you have already done.

learnableGaps.label: Translation or localisation tooling
learnableGaps.note: Tooling only — this board does not surface language-focused roles, but a passing tool requirement should not sink an otherwise good posting.

disqualifying.label: A credential you do not hold
A management remit rather than hands-on review

_lifestyleComment: LIFESTYLE FIT — the spec's special positive signals. The location gate has already dropped anything that is not remote, so this axis is about how much freedom the posting actually offers on top of that: contract and project framing, part-time and flexible capacity, asynchronous work, and pay that is stated rather than hidden.
_industriesComment: The spec's industry positives. Small, deliberate weights: a good posting from an unlisted industry should not lose to a mediocre one from a listed one.
_thinPostingComment: Jooble and the RSS feeds return a two-line snippet rather than a description, and three of the four axes read the description — so a posting titled exactly what she is looking for can arrive scoring like a mediocre one purely because there is nothing to read. A posting shorter than minChars whose title names a family, with nothing counting against it, is floored on the strength of the title alone, and the card says the score was read off a snippet.
_seniorityComment: Read off the job title only, and used by the board's 👍/👎 ranking model to make sense of a 'too senior' or 'too junior' rating. Descriptions mention senior stakeholders constantly; the title is what states the level of the job being advertised.
_discoveryComment: The spec's instruction to flag unusual opportunities even when the score is lower, because they may reveal a career category she would not have searched. A posting qualifies when its title belongs to an adjacent family, or when it wants enough distinct abilities with no recognisable title at all.
